Patient Information

Treating Insomnia

What actually works for persistent insomnia — the behavioural treatment that outperforms sleeping tablets, relaxation techniques, sleep hygiene, daytime activity and pain control.

Almost everyone sleeps badly at some point. Insomnia becomes a condition when the difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early has persisted for three months or more, happens at least three nights a week, and affects your days as well as your nights.

By that stage, whatever started it — an illness, a bereavement, pain, shift work, a stressful year — is usually no longer what is keeping it going. What keeps it going is the set of sensible-seeming things people do in response: going to bed earlier to catch up, lying there trying hard to sleep, napping, cancelling plans, and watching the clock. The treatment works by undoing those, and it is more effective than any sleeping tablet.

If you read nothing else

Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia — the combination of the sleep window, stimulus control, cognitive work and relaxation set out below — is recommended as the first-line treatment ahead of medication by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the American College of Physicians. Its effects are comparable to sleeping tablets in the short term and, unlike tablets, they persist after the treatment stops.

How to use this sheet
  • Read it once through, then start with the first two or three exercises only.
  • Add an exercise every week or two rather than starting everything at once.
  • Print it, tick off the days, and bring it back to your appointment.
  • This sheet is general information for my patients. If you have been given different, specific advice about your own condition, that advice comes first.

Why it has not settled on its own

Three things combine to produce chronic insomnia. The first two are history; the third is what we treat.

🧬 What you brought to it

Some people are simply built to sleep more lightly — a family tendency, a tendency to worry, an alert nervous system. This is not your fault and it is not something we can change. It is background, not cause.

⚡ What set it off

An illness, an operation, pain, grief, menopause, a stressful period, a new baby, night shifts. The trigger is often long gone by the time people seek help — which is exactly why 'the stress has passed, so why am I still not sleeping?' is such a common question.

🔁 What keeps it going

Extra time in bed, daytime naps, trying hard to sleep, clock-watching, anxiety about tomorrow, and the bed itself becoming a cue for frustration. These are the treatable part, and every technique below targets one of them.

Step 1 — Measure it

Two weeks of a simple diary. Everything else is set from these numbers.

Step 0 — Two weeks of a sleep diary

Every morning for 2 weeks, takes 2 minutes
Do this before anything else

Everything else on this page depends on knowing what your sleep is actually doing. Memory is a poor guide: most people with insomnia underestimate how much they sleep and overestimate how long they lie awake.

  1. Each morning, write down: what time you went to bed, roughly how long it took to fall asleep, how many times you woke and for roughly how long, what time you finally woke, and what time you got out of bed.
  2. Add a line for daytime naps, alcohol, caffeine after midday, and any sleeping tablet.
  3. Estimate, do not measure. Do not clock-watch during the night, and turn the clock face away from you.
  4. At the end of each week, add up your average time in bed and your average actual sleep time.
  5. Divide sleep time by time in bed and multiply by 100 — that is your sleep efficiency, and it is the number that drives the treatment below.
Make it harderKeep it going through the first month of treatment, so you can see the change rather than guess at it.
Make it easierIf a paper diary is a burden, a note on your phone each morning is fine. Sleep-tracking watches and rings are not a substitute and often make things worse by fuelling anxiety about the numbers.
SafetyNone — but if the diary shows loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, or falling asleep during the day despite adequate time in bed, tell me before starting sleep-window therapy.
Why it worksThe sleep diary is the standard measurement tool in every trial of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, and clinicians use it to set and adjust the treatment.

Step 2 — The two techniques that do most of the work

These are the hard ones and the effective ones. Expect three to six weeks before the benefit is clear.

Stimulus control — rebuilding the bed–sleep connection

Every night, without exception, for at least 4 weeks
First-line CBT-I component

After months of lying awake, your bed becomes a cue for frustrated wakefulness instead of sleep. These six rules break that association. They are simple, they are hard, and they work.

  1. Go to bed only when you are sleepy — not merely tired, but genuinely nodding off. Being 'ready for bed' is not the same as being sleepy.
  2. Use the bed only for sleep and sex. No reading, television, phone, laptop, radio, or worrying in bed.
  3. If you are awake for what feels like 15–20 minutes, get up. Leave the bedroom. Sit somewhere else in dim light and do something quiet and undemanding until you feel sleepy, then return to bed.
  4. Repeat that as often as necessary, even five times a night. This is the hard part and it is the part that works.
  5. Get up at the same time every morning, seven days a week, regardless of how badly you slept. The morning alarm anchors the whole rhythm.
  6. Do not nap. If you must, keep it under 20 minutes and before 3 pm.
Make it harderNone — these rules do not change. They become easier by about the second or third week, and the improvement usually follows in weeks three to six.
Make it easierIf getting out of bed is impractical — because of pain, cold, or unsteadiness — sit up out of the covers, or move to a chair in the bedroom instead. The principle is 'do not lie in bed awake and frustrated'.
SafetyIf you are unsteady on your feet at night, put a light on before getting up, and keep the path clear. Falls at night in the dark are common and serious.
Why it worksStimulus control is one of the two components that carry most of the effect of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, which is recommended as first-line treatment ahead of medication by both the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2021) and the American College of Physicians.

Sleep window therapy (sleep restriction)

Reset weekly, based on your diary
The most powerful single component

Lying in bed for nine hours to catch six hours of sleep spreads the sleep thin and broken. Compressing time in bed makes sleep deeper, more continuous and more reliable — then the window is widened again.

  1. From your two-week diary, work out your average actual sleep time per night. Say it is 5 hours 30 minutes.
  2. That, plus about 30 minutes, becomes your time in bed — your sleep window. Never set it below 5 hours.
  3. Fix your rising time first, at whatever time you must be up. Then count backwards to set your bedtime. If your window is 6 hours and you must rise at 6:30 am, you go to bed at 12:30 am — and not before, no matter how tired you feel.
  4. Keep the same window every night, weekends included, for a week.
  5. At the end of the week, work out your sleep efficiency (sleep time ÷ time in bed × 100). If it is 90% or more, move your bedtime 15 minutes earlier. If it is 85–89%, change nothing. If it is below 85%, move your bedtime 15 minutes later.
  6. Repeat every week until you reach a window that gives you good sleep efficiency and you feel rested.
Make it harderThe window widens by 15 minutes a week as your sleep consolidates. Most people finish somewhere between 6.5 and 7.5 hours.
Make it easierIf the full method is too harsh, a gentler version — simply not going to bed before a fixed time, and always rising at the same time — captures much of the benefit.
SafetyThis makes you sleepier during the first one to two weeks. Do not start it in a week when you must drive long distances, operate machinery, or work night shifts, and stop driving if you feel sleepy at the wheel. Tell me first if you have epilepsy, bipolar disorder, or untreated sleep apnoea — sleep restriction can destabilise all three and needs supervision.
Why it worksSleep restriction is the most potent single element of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia. In the HABIT trial (The Lancet, 2023), practice nurses with no previous sleep training delivered four brief sessions of sleep restriction therapy in UK general practice, and it significantly reduced insomnia severity compared with sleep hygiene advice — an effect that was still present six and twelve months later.
The first fortnight is the worst of it

Sleep window therapy makes you sleepier before it makes you better — that is the mechanism, not a sign it is failing. Sleep becomes deeper and less broken first, and only then does the amount increase. Start it in a fortnight where you can afford to be tired, do not start it the week before a long drive, and hold your nerve at day four when it feels pointless. Most people who abandon the treatment abandon it in the first ten days.

Step 3 — Turning the arousal down

Insomnia is a state of being too alert at the wrong time. These are the techniques that address it directly — practise them by day, so they work at night.

Slow breathing

5–10 minutes, twice a day plus at bedtime
Relaxation — start here

Slowing the breath is the quickest reliable way to shift the body out of alert mode. It is the foundation of every other relaxation technique, and the easiest to learn.

  1. Lie on your back or sit comfortably. Put one hand on your chest and one on your belly.
  2. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of four, letting the hand on your belly rise while the hand on your chest stays still.
  3. Breathe out slowly through your mouth or nose for a count of six. The out-breath being longer than the in-breath is the important part.
  4. Continue at about six breaths a minute. Do not force a big breath — this is slow and soft, not deep and effortful.
  5. When your mind wanders — it will — simply notice and return to the counting. That returning is the practice, not a failure of it.
  6. Practise it during the day as well as at night. A technique first attempted at 3 am rarely works.
Make it harderLengthen the out-breath to a count of eight. Add a word on the out-breath such as 'calm', or count each breath backwards from 20.
Make it easierDo 2 minutes rather than 10. Or simply make every out-breath a little longer than the in-breath, without counting at all.
SafetyIf you feel light-headed or tingly, you are breathing too deeply — make the breaths smaller and slower.
Why it worksRelaxation training is a recognised component of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, most useful for people whose insomnia is driven by physical tension and racing thoughts. There is a fuller step-by-step version on my stress management page.

Progressive muscle relaxation

15 minutes daily; a shortened version at bedtime
Best for physical tension

Tense muscles keep the nervous system alert. Deliberately tensing and then releasing each muscle group teaches you what relaxed actually feels like — most people with chronic tension have lost the ability to recognise it.

  1. Lie down somewhere warm and quiet, and take three slow breaths.
  2. Starting with your feet: curl your toes and tense the muscles hard for 5 seconds — about three-quarters effort, not maximal.
  3. Release suddenly and completely, and spend 15–20 seconds noticing the difference between the tense state and the released one. That contrast is the whole technique.
  4. Work upwards in turn: calves, thighs, buttocks, stomach, hands (clench the fists), forearms, upper arms, shoulders (shrug to the ears), neck, jaw (clench gently), and finally the face (screw it up).
  5. Finish by lying still for a minute, breathing slowly, letting everything feel heavy.
  6. Once you have practised this for two or three weeks, learn the short version: tense the whole body at once for 5 seconds, release, and repeat three times.
Make it harderMove to 'release-only' relaxation — going through the same muscle groups and simply letting go of each, without tensing first. This is the version you can use anywhere, including in bed.
Make it easierDo the upper body only, seated. Skip any muscle group that hurts.
SafetyDo not tense a painful, injured or recently operated area, and go gently on the neck and back. If you have cramps, reduce the tensing effort.
Why it worksProgressive muscle relaxation dates to Jacobson's work in the 1930s and remains one of the best-studied relaxation methods for insomnia and anxiety. Step-by-step instructions are also on my stress management page.

Body scan and mindful attention

10–20 minutes, daily practice
Best for a racing mind

Gives an overactive mind something undemanding to rest on. The aim is not to force sleep — it is to stop the effortful struggle that keeps you awake.

  1. Lie comfortably and close your eyes.
  2. Move your attention slowly through the body, starting at the toes of one foot: simply notice whatever is there — warmth, coolness, pressure, tingling, or nothing at all.
  3. Spend perhaps 20 seconds on each area and move steadily up through the body to the top of the head.
  4. You are not trying to relax the area or change anything. You are only noticing, without judging.
  5. When you realise you have been lost in thought, note where the mind went, and return to where you were. This will happen many times a session.
  6. If you fall asleep during it, that is a welcome side effect, not the goal.
Make it harderExtend to 30 minutes; add a formal daily mindfulness practice; consider a structured mindfulness course.
Make it easierScan only from the feet to the hips, or use a guided audio recording.
SafetyA few people find turning attention inwards uncomfortable, particularly after trauma. If it increases distress, use the breathing or muscle relaxation methods instead.
Why it worksMindfulness-based approaches improve insomnia and are a reasonable alternative for people who find the structure of cognitive behavioural therapy difficult, though the evidence base is smaller.
A fuller guide to these techniques

My separate page on stress management takes you through the same relaxation techniques in more detail, including the breathing and progressive muscle relaxation practices referred to here.

Step 4 — The mind at 2 am

For the racing thoughts, the problem-solving, and the arithmetic of how many hours are left.

Constructive worry — putting the day down

15 minutes, early evening, daily
For the 2 am problem-solving mind

Bed is the first quiet moment of the day, so the mind uses it to review problems. Giving worry a proper slot earlier in the evening reliably reduces how much of it turns up at bedtime.

  1. At least two hours before bed, sit at a table with a notebook — not in the bedroom.
  2. Draw a line down the middle. On the left, write down everything on your mind. On the right, write the single next step for each, and when you will do it.
  3. For things with no next step — the genuinely uncontrollable — write 'nothing to do tonight' beside them. That is a legitimate and useful answer.
  4. Close the notebook. It is now on paper and does not need to be held in your head.
  5. If a worry surfaces in bed anyway, say to yourself: 'that is on the list, it is dealt with tomorrow', and return to your breathing.
  6. Keep a pad by the bed for anything genuinely new — write it down in the dark, and let it go.
Make it harderAdd a short gratitude or 'what went well' list at the end — a deliberate change of mental gear before bed.
Make it easierJust the list, no columns.
SafetyNone.
Why it worksStructured worry time is a standard cognitive technique in insomnia treatment, targeting the pre-sleep cognitive arousal that most patients describe as 'my mind won't switch off'.

Challenging the thoughts that keep you awake

Ongoing, whenever the thought appears
Cognitive therapy

Insomnia is maintained by a small set of beliefs — 'I must get eight hours', 'tomorrow will be ruined', 'I have no control over this'. These beliefs create the anxiety that prevents the sleep, and the prophecy fulfils itself.

  1. Notice the thought and write it down exactly as it occurs to you: 'if I don't sleep tonight I won't cope tomorrow'.
  2. Ask: what is the evidence? Look back over your diary at the days after your worst nights. Did you actually fail to cope, or did you get through a below-par day?
  3. Ask: what is a more accurate version? For example — 'tomorrow will be harder than I would like, and I have got through many such days before'.
  4. Correct the arithmetic. Sleep need varies: many healthy adults need seven hours, some need six, and normal sleep includes brief awakenings you would not remember when you were sleeping well.
  5. Drop the effort. Trying to sleep is the one activity guaranteed to prevent it. Aim only to rest quietly — if you are willing to be awake, you will usually fall asleep.
Make it harderSet yourself a behavioural test: deliberately keep a normal day's plans after a bad night, and check whether the catastrophe you predicted actually happened.
Make it easierUse the single most useful reframe: 'rest is valuable too, and my body will take the sleep it needs eventually'.
SafetyNone.
Why it worksCognitive restructuring targets the dysfunctional beliefs about sleep that maintain insomnia, and paradoxical intention — giving up the effort to sleep — is itself a recommended technique with trial support.

Step 5 — The day, not the night

Sleep is built during the day. These three are the ones patients most often have back to front.

Building sleep pressure during the day

30 minutes of activity most days + morning light
Often the missing piece

Sleep at night is built during the day. Two things generate it: physical activity, and enough hours of continuous wakefulness. Sitting all day and dozing in the evening dismantles both.

  1. Move every day. Aim for 30 minutes of moderate activity — brisk walking counts — on most days. Break it up if you need to.
  2. Get outside within an hour or two of waking, for at least 20–30 minutes. Morning daylight is the strongest signal setting your body clock, and it is many times brighter outdoors than in any lit room, even on an overcast day.
  3. Do not doze in the evening chair. An evening nap in front of the television discharges exactly the sleep pressure you need at bedtime. If you find yourself nodding off at 8 pm, stand up and do something.
  4. Keep the evening dimmer. Lower the lights in the last hour, which supports the natural rise in melatonin.
  5. Do not exercise vigorously in the last hour before bed if it keeps you awake — though the evidence is that for most people, evening exercise does not harm sleep, and the old blanket warning was overstated. Judge it on your own experience.
Make it harderAdd a second daylight walk in the late afternoon. Increase the intensity of the daily activity.
Make it easierEven 10 minutes outdoors in the morning and a short walk after lunch will help.
SafetyIf you are unsteady, see the balance sheets on this site before increasing outdoor walking.
Why it worksMeta-analyses of exercise trials in people with insomnia show moderate improvements in sleep quality and time to fall asleep. Regular timing of light, activity and meals reinforces the circadian rhythm that insomnia typically erodes.

Sleep hygiene — necessary but not sufficient

Daily habits
Read the caveat

These are the background conditions for sleep. They are worth getting right — but be clear that on its own, sleep hygiene advice is a weak treatment for established insomnia. It is the floor, not the building.

  1. Caffeine: none after midday. Its half-life is around five to six hours, and longer with age, so a 3 pm coffee is still working at midnight. Remember tea, cola, energy drinks and dark chocolate.
  2. Alcohol: it shortens the time to fall asleep and then fragments the second half of the night, suppresses REM sleep and worsens snoring and apnoea. It is one of the most common causes of 3 am waking.
  3. Nicotine is a stimulant, and overnight withdrawal wakes people.
  4. The bedroom: cool (around 18°C), dark, quiet. Your core temperature must fall for sleep to begin, which is also why a warm bath 1–2 hours before bed helps — the warming is followed by a drop.
  5. Screens: the content matters more than the light. A work email or an argument on social media is far more arousing than the screen's brightness. Keep the phone out of the bedroom, and use an ordinary alarm clock.
  6. Food: avoid a heavy meal in the two hours before bed, but do not go to bed hungry.
  7. Fluids: taper drinks in the evening if you are up to the toilet at night.
Make it harderOnce these are in place, put your effort into stimulus control and the sleep window — that is where the results come from.
Make it easierPick the two that most obviously apply to you rather than attempting all of them.
SafetyDo not stop a regular sleeping tablet abruptly to 'do this properly' — benzodiazepines and z-drugs must be tapered, and rebound insomnia after sudden withdrawal is severe. Talk to me or your GP first.
Why it worksThis is the point most often missed. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2021 guideline gives a strong recommendation for multicomponent cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, and explicitly does not recommend sleep hygiene education as a treatment on its own, for lack of evidence that it works. It is so weak that trials routinely use it as the control condition against which real treatments are measured.

Getting pain under control at night

Plan the evening deliberately
Two-way street

Pain fragments sleep, and poor sleep lowers the pain threshold the following day — a loop that tightens over months. Neither problem is fully treatable while the other is ignored.

  1. Time your analgesia to cover the night, not just the evening. If a dose wears off at 3 am, that is when you will wake — discuss the timing and the preparation with me or your GP rather than simply taking more.
  2. Set up the bed for the painful part. For back pain, a pillow under the knees when lying on your back, or between the knees when on your side. For neck pain, one pillow supporting the hollow of the neck rather than a stack propping the head forward, and no sleeping on your front.
  3. Do the gentle exercises from the relevant sheet in the evening, not just the morning — stiffness that has built through the day is what wakes you at 2 am.
  4. Use heat before bed if it helps — a warm shower or heat pack has the added benefit of the temperature drop that follows.
  5. Apply the same relaxation techniques to the pain. Slow breathing and progressive muscle relaxation reduce the muscle guarding that amplifies pain, and reduce the distress that makes it harder to bear.
  6. Expect to be more sensitive after a bad night, and do not read that as your condition deteriorating.
Make it harderIf pain is the dominant barrier, cognitive behavioural approaches for pain and for insomnia can be combined, and are more effective together than either alone.
Make it easierStart with a single change: the pillow arrangement, or the timing of the last dose.
SafetyBe cautious with sedating painkillers as sleeping aids. Opioids fragment sleep architecture and worsen sleep apnoea; combining them with sleeping tablets is genuinely dangerous.
Why it worksThe relationship between sleep and pain is bidirectional, and evidence suggests poor sleep predicts next-day pain more strongly than pain predicts that night's sleep — which is an argument for treating the insomnia in its own right rather than waiting for the pain to settle.

Where medication fits

Tablets are not forbidden, and there are situations where they are the right answer. But they work best as a short bridge, and they treat the symptom rather than the mechanism. Nothing here is a recommendation for you personally — that is a conversation for the consulting room.

💊 Benzodiazepines and 'z-drugs'

Temazepam, zolpidem, zopiclone and their relatives. Effective for a few nights, and reasonable for a short, defined crisis. Beyond a few weeks, tolerance develops, sleep quality deteriorates, and stopping causes rebound insomnia that feels like proof you still need them. In older adults they raise the risk of falls, fractures, confusion and car accidents. Never stop one abruptly — they must be tapered slowly, and doing that alongside CBT-I is far more successful than doing it alone.

🌙 Melatonin

Weak as a sleeping tablet, useful as a body-clock signal. Prolonged-release melatonin is approved in Australia for people over 55, and immediate-release melatonin at a low dose, taken several hours before bed, is genuinely useful for delayed sleep timing and for jet lag. Do not expect a sedative effect.

🧪 The newer orexin blockers

Suvorexant, lemborexant and daridorexant work by blocking the brain's wake-promoting orexin system rather than by sedating you. They appear to cause less tolerance and less rebound than the older drugs, and are a reasonable option where medication is genuinely needed. Availability and cost in Australia vary — worth discussing.

🌀 Sedating antidepressants

Low-dose doxepin has good evidence specifically for staying asleep. Amitriptyline and mirtazapine are widely used, help where pain or depression coexist, and carry their own burdens — dry mouth, constipation, weight gain, next-day grogginess. Anticholinergic drugs deserve particular caution in older people.

⚠️ Quetiapine and antihistamines

Quetiapine is commonly prescribed for sleep and is not recommended for insomnia: the evidence is poor and the metabolic and movement side effects are real. Over-the-counter antihistamine sleep aids (doxylamine, diphenhydramine) cause tolerance within days and next-day impairment, and are poorly suited to older adults.

🍷 Alcohol and cannabis

Both are widely used as sleeping aids and both make sleep worse over time. Alcohol fragments the second half of the night and worsens sleep apnoea. Cannabis suppresses dreaming sleep, and stopping after regular use causes several nights of markedly disturbed sleep — which tends to drive people back to it.

Before you accept the label 'insomnia'

Several conditions masquerade as insomnia and will not respond to any of the above. Any of these is worth raising with me.

😮‍💨 Obstructive sleep apnoea

Loud snoring, witnessed pauses, waking unrefreshed, morning headache, dozing off during the day, waking with a start or gasping. It coexists with insomnia far more often than people expect, and treating the insomnia alone will fail.

🦵 Restless legs syndrome

An irresistible urge to move the legs, worse in the evening and at rest, relieved by moving. Very treatable — and low iron stores are a common, correctable cause, so ferritin is worth checking.

🥊 Acting out dreams

Shouting, punching or kicking during sleep, sometimes injuring a bed partner. This is REM sleep behaviour disorder, and it is important both to treat and to investigate. Tell me if your partner has described this.

🕐 A body clock in the wrong place

If you cannot fall asleep before 2 am but sleep perfectly well until 10 am, that is a circadian rhythm problem, not insomnia — and the treatment is timed light and melatonin, not sleeping tablets.

🌧️ Depression and anxiety

Early morning waking with low mood, or a mind that will not stop at night. Insomnia and depression each worsen the other, and treating the insomnia in its own right improves the depression as well.

🚽 Nocturia and menopause

Being woken repeatedly by the bladder, or by hot flushes, is not insomnia — it is a different problem with different treatments, and both are common causes of what gets labelled as insomnia in mid and later life.

Questions people ask me

"How much sleep do I actually need?"

Less than you have probably been told. Adult sleep need is a range — most people fall between seven and nine hours, some function perfectly on six, and the requirement falls a little with age. The right amount is the amount that leaves you able to function, not a number you have read.

Chasing 'eight hours' is itself a common perpetuator of insomnia: it produces extra time in bed, which produces broken sleep.

"My smartwatch says I get almost no deep sleep."

Consumer sleep trackers estimate sleep stages from movement and heart rate, and they are unreliable at exactly the thing they are being trusted for. Their commonest effect in people with insomnia is to increase anxiety about sleep, which worsens it — there is even a name for it. Use a diary of how you feel, and if you want to keep the watch, stop reading the sleep score.

"Isn't sleep hygiene the treatment?"

No, and this matters. Sleep hygiene advice on its own is a weak treatment for established insomnia — so weak that it is routinely used as the control condition in trials of real treatments. Get the basics right, then put your effort into stimulus control and the sleep window, which is where the results come from.

"What if I just cannot get out of bed at 3 am?"

Then sit up, out of the covers, with a low light on and something undemanding to read. The principle is to break the association between the bed and lying there frustrated — the getting up is the usual way to do it, not the only way. If you are unsteady on your feet, put the light on first.

"Will one bad night hurt me?"

No. The health headlines about sleep and dementia, heart disease and cancer are mostly about years of short sleep, and they frighten people with insomnia into precisely the anxiety that maintains it. A bad night makes for a below-par day. Your body compensates: sleep after a poor night is deeper and more efficient, which is exactly the mechanism the sleep window uses deliberately.

"How long until this works?"

Most people see a clear change between weeks three and six, and the benefit continues to build for months afterwards. Judge it at six weeks, not at six days — and expect the improvement to look like more solid sleep before it looks like more sleep.

Making it actually happen

The best programme is the one you will still be doing in three months. These are the things that reliably make the difference.

🔗 Attach it to something you already do

Balance work while the kettle boils. Neck exercises after brushing your teeth. Relaxation practice as you get into bed. A new habit hooked onto an old one survives; a new habit floating free does not.

📅 Keep a tick sheet

A calendar on the fridge with a tick for each day. Self-monitoring is one of the few adherence strategies with consistent evidence behind it, and it gives us something real to look at in clinic.

🎯 Set a specific, checkable goal

Not 'improve my balance', but 'stand on one leg for 30 seconds each side by the end of March', or 'walk to the shops and back without stopping'. Write it down.

⏱️ Ten minutes beats an hour you never start

Short daily sessions beat one long weekly effort. The programmes below are designed to be done in ten to twenty minutes, most days, in your own kitchen or hallway.

Almost every trial that produced a real result ran for at least eight to twelve weeks. Judge the programme at three months, not at three days.

Getting more help in Australia

Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the treatment with the best evidence, and there are several ways to get it.

💻 Online CBT-I programmes

Structured digital programmes deliver the same components as face-to-face therapy — sleep window, stimulus control, cognitive work — and have good trial evidence. They are the most practical option for most people: no waiting list, done at your own pace. Australian and international programmes are available; ask me which I currently recommend.

🧠 A psychologist trained in CBT-I

Your GP can prepare a Mental Health Treatment Plan giving Medicare-rebated sessions with a psychologist. Ask specifically for someone who does CBT for insomnia — it is a particular protocol, not general counselling, and typically takes four to eight sessions.

🩺 Your GP

The right person to review your medications, check thyroid function, iron studies (low ferritin drives restless legs), mood, menopause symptoms and pain control, and to arrange a sleep study if one is needed.

😴 A sleep physician and a sleep study

Worth arranging if there is loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, unrefreshing sleep despite adequate hours, marked daytime sleepiness, restless legs, or acting out of dreams. Insomnia that has not responded to proper CBT-I is also a reason to look again.

Tell me, or your GP, if
  • You fall asleep unintentionally during the day — while driving, in conversation, at meals.
  • Your partner describes snoring with pauses in breathing, gasping, or acting out dreams.
  • You are having thoughts of harming yourself, or your mood is persistently low.
  • You are using alcohol, cannabis or increasing doses of a sleeping tablet to get to sleep.
  • You want to stop a regular sleeping tablet — this needs a planned taper, not an abrupt stop.
  • The insomnia has not budged after a proper attempt at the programme above.
  • You have new headaches, seizures, or unusual behaviour at night.
